title: The Five Levels of Hukm Taklifi
summary: The fiqh scale that every Islamic ruling on an action sits on, from obligatory to forbidden — and why most of daily life falls in the wide middle ground.

body.text: A five-point scale, not just "halal or haram"

New Muslims often start out sorting everything into two bins: halal (allowed) and haram (forbidden). Islamic legal theory (Usul al-Fiqh) actually uses a five-point scale called Hukm Taklifi ("the ruling that places a duty on a person") to classify any action. Knowing the full scale removes a lot of unnecessary anxiety, since most everyday actions sit in the wide, comfortable middle — and it's the framework behind Stage 3's closer look at what actually makes something halal or haram.
1. Wajib / Fard (obligatory) — required; a Muslim is rewarded for doing it and sinful for neglecting it without valid excuse. The five daily prayers and Zakat are wajib.
2. Mustahabb / Mandub / Sunnah (recommended) — encouraged and rewarded, but not sinful to skip. Extra voluntary prayers and many of the Prophet's personal habits fall here.
3. Mubah (permissible) — neutral; neither rewarded nor blamed either way. Most ordinary choices — what to eat for breakfast, which career to pursue, how to decorate a room — are mubah.
4. Makruh (disliked) — discouraged and best avoided, but not sinful. Excessive minor waste, or interrupting someone's speech unnecessarily, are commonly cited as makruh.
5. Haram (forbidden) — prohibited; sinful to do, and avoided for reward. Consuming alcohol and lying are haram.

body.translation: Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear.

body.text: A common source of unnecessary stress for new Muslims is assuming that if something isn't clearly "good," it must be bad. In reality, the vast majority of daily choices are mubah — genuinely open, with no religious weight attached either way. Recognising that gives real freedom: Islam regulates specific matters carefully, but it doesn't turn every decision into a moral test.

body.question: How do I find out which category something falls into?
body.answer: For major, well-known matters (the Five Pillars, the well-known prohibitions), it's usually obvious or already covered elsewhere in this app. For anything more specific or unfamiliar, asking a knowledgeable local teacher or a reputable Q&A source is the right move — this scale is a framework for understanding answers, not a tool for working them out alone from first principles.

body.question: Do scholars ever disagree about which category something belongs in?
body.answer: Yes, especially for makruh versus haram, or mustahabb versus wajib, on specific secondary matters — this is part of the same legitimate scholarly difference of opinion covered in the Madhhabs lesson, not a contradiction in the religion itself.

body.question: Does realising how much of daily life falls under "mubah" — genuinely neutral — change how much pressure you feel about getting every choice "right"?
